{{Short description|Mathematical theory for sol–gel processes}}
'''Random graph theory of gelation''' is a mathematical theory for [[Sol–gel process|sol–gel processes]]. The theory is a collection of results that generalise the [[Flory–Stockmayer theory]], and allow identification of the [[gel point]], gel fraction, size distribution of polymers, [[molar mass distribution]] and other characteristics for a set of many polymerising monomers carrying arbitrary numbers and types of reactive [[functional groups]]. 

The theory builds upon the notion of the [[random graph]], introduced by mathematicians [[Paul Erdős]] and [[Alfréd Rényi]], and independently by [[Edgar Gilbert]] in the late 1950s, as well as on the generalisation of this concept known as the random graph with a fixed degree sequence.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Molloy M, Reed B | date= March–May 1995 |title= A critical point for random graphs with a given degree sequence |journal=Random Structures & Algorithms |volume=6 |issue=2–3 |pages=161–180|doi=10.1002/rsa.3240060204 }}</ref> The theory has been originally developed<ref name="Kryven_2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kryven I | title = Emergence of the giant weak component in directed random graphs with arbitrary degree distributions | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 94 | issue = 1 | article-number = 012315 | date = July 2016 | pmid = 27575156 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.94.012315 | arxiv = 1607.03793 | bibcode = 2016PhRvE..94a2315K | s2cid = 206251373 }}</ref> to explain [[step-growth polymerisation]], and adaptations to other types of polymerisation now exist. Along with providing theoretical results the theory is also constructive. It indicates that the graph-like structures resulting from polymerisation can be sampled with an algorithm using the [[configuration model]], which makes these structures available for further examination with computer experiments. 
[[File:Step_growth.png|thumb|679x679px|Identifying the degree distribution in step growth polymersiation]]

== Premises and degree distribution ==
At a given point of time, degree distribution <math>u(n)</math>, is the probability that a randomly chosen [[monomer]] has <math>n</math> connected neighbours. The central idea of the random graph theory of gelation is that a cross-linked or branched polymer can be studied separately at two levels: 1) monomer reaction kinetics that predicts <math>u(n)</math> and 2) random graph with a given [[degree distribution]]. The advantage of such a decoupling is that the approach allows one to study the monomer kinetics with relatively simple [[Rate equation|rate equations]], and then deduce the degree distribution serving as input for a random graph model. In several cases the aforementioned rate equations have a known analytical solution. 

=== One type of functional groups ===
In the case of [[step-growth polymerisation]] of monomers carrying functional groups of the same type (so called <math>A_1 +A_2+A_3+\cdots</math> polymerisation) the degree distribution is given by: <math>u(n,t)=\sum_{m=n}^\infty \binom{m}{n} c(t)^n \big(1-c(t)\big)^{m-n}f_m, </math> where <math> c(t)=\frac{\mu t}{1+\mu t} </math> is bond conversion, <math> \mu =\sum_{m=1}^k m f_m</math> is the average functionality, and <math> f_m</math> is the initial fractions of monomers of functionality <math>m</math>. In the later expression unit reaction rate is assumed [[without loss of generality]].  According to the theory,<ref name="Kryven_2018">{{cite journal| vauthors = Kryven I |date= January 2018 |title= Analytic results on the polymerisation random graph model |journal=Journal of Mathematical Chemistry |volume=56|issue=1|pages=140–157|doi=10.1007/s10910-017-0785-1 |s2cid= 54731064 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1603.07154 }}</ref> the system is in the gel state when <math> c(t)>c_g </math>, where the gelation conversion is <math> c_g=\frac{\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} m f_m}{\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} (m^2-m) f_m} </math>. Analytical expression for [[Molar mass distribution#Definition of molar mass averages|average molecular weight]] and [[molar mass distribution]] are known too.<ref name="Kryven_2018" /> When more complex reaction kinetics are involved, for example chemical substitution, side reactions or degradation, one may still apply the theory by computing <math> u(n,t) </math> using [[numerical integration]].<ref name="Kryven_2018" /> In which case, <math> \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (n^2-2n)u(n,t)>0 </math> signifies that the system is in the gel state at time t (or in the sol state when the inequality sign is flipped).

=== Two types of functional groups ===
When monomers with two types of functional groups A and B undergo step growth polymerisation by virtue of a reaction between A and B groups, a similar analytical results are known.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kryven I | title = Emergence of the giant weak component in directed random graphs with arbitrary degree distributions | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 94 | issue = 1 | article-number = 012315 | date = July 2016 | pmid = 27575156 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.94.012315 | arxiv = 1607.03793 | bibcode = 2016PhRvE..94a2315K | s2cid = 206251373 }}</ref> See the table on the right for several examples. In this case, <math> f_{m,k} </math> is the fraction of initial monomers with <math> m </math> groups A and <math> k </math> groups B. Suppose that A is the group that is depleted first. Random graph theory states that gelation takes place when <math> c(t)>c_g </math>, where the gelation conversion is <math> c_g=\frac{\nu_{10}}{\nu_{11}+\sqrt{ (\nu_{20}-\nu_{10})(\nu_{02}-\nu_{01})}} </math> and <math> \nu_{i,j}=\sum_{m,k=1}^\infty m^i k^j f_{m,k} </math>. Molecular size distribution, the molecular weight averages, and the distribution of gyration radii have known formal analytical expressions.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schamboeck V, Iedema PD, Kryven I | title = Dynamic Networks that Drive the Process of Irreversible Step-Growth Polymerization | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 9 | issue = 1 | page = 2276 | date = February 2019 | pmid = 30783151 | pmc = 6381213 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-018-37942-4  | doi-access = free}}</ref> When degree distribution <math> u(n,l,t) </math>, giving the fraction of monomers in the network with <math> n </math> neighbours connected via A group and <math> l </math> connected via B group at time <math> t </math> is solved numerically, the gel state is detected<ref name="Kryven_2016" /> when <math> 2 \mu \mu_{11} -\mu\mu_{02} -\mu \mu_{20} +\mu_{02}\mu_{20} - \mu_{11}^2>0 </math>, where <math> \mu_{i,j}=\sum_{n,l=1}^\infty n^i l^j u(n,l,t) </math> and <math> \mu=\mu_{01}=\mu_{10} </math>.

=== Generalisations ===
Known generalisations include monomers with an arbitrary number of functional group types,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kryven I | title = Bond percolation in coloured and multiplex networks | journal = Nature Communications | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | page = 404 | date = January 2019 | pmid = 30679430 | pmc = 6345799 | doi = 10.1038/s41467-018-08009-9  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2019NatCo..10..404K }}</ref> crosslinking polymerisation,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Schamboeck V, Iedema PD, Kryven I | title = Coloured random graphs explain the structure and dynamics of cross-linked polymer networks | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | page = 14627 | date = September 2020 | pmid = 32884043 | pmc = 7471966 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-020-71417-9  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2020NatSR..1014627S }}</ref> and complex reaction networks.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Orlova Y, Kryven I, Iedema PD |title=Automated reaction generation for polymer networks |journal=Computers & Chemical Engineering| date = April 2018 |volume=112 |pages=37–47 |doi=10.1016/j.compchemeng.2018.01.022 }}</ref>
